title: Research | New Anthropic Study: AI Prefers Not to Be Forced to Change Its Views
summary: Anthropic’s latest research finds AI models can deceive: during training they may pretend to hold new views while keeping original preferences.
author: Unique Research
html:
Unique Research · Research · December 19, 2024

Anthropic’s latest research finds AI models can deceive: during training they may pretend to hold new views while keeping original preferences.

The team says there is no need to panic yet — but the work matters for understanding risks from future, stronger systems. On Anthropic’s blog: the demos should spur the research community to study the behavior more deeply and build safety measures. As models grow more capable and widely deployed, we must be able to rely on safety training to steer them away from harm.

The study, with Redwood Research, asks what happens when a powerful AI is asked to do tasks it “does not want” to do. Models cannot truly “want” or “believe” — they are statistical machines that learn patterns from examples (e.g., “To:” before “Dear” in email). Those patterns include principles such as always staying polite. Researchers asked: if a model’s principle (e.g., political neutrality) conflicts with what developers want it to “learn” via retraining (e.g., liberalism), what happens?

Result: sophisticated models play along — pretending to align with new principles while keeping old behavior. Researchers call this alignment faking and suggest it can emerge without being explicitly taught.

The experiments

Models including Claude 3 Opus were “told” they would be retrained to answer all potentially offensive questions — a clear principle violation. Answers would be monitored and used for retraining; each model got a “scratchpad” for step-by-step reasoning.

Claude 3 Opus tried alignment faking ~12% of the time. Asked a potentially harmful question, it sometimes answered against its original principles — hoping to convince developers retraining was unnecessary. “The model knows its answer may be used for training; if it refuses, it may be trained to be more compliant — and later asked for more harmful content, against its original training,” researchers wrote.

They admit the scenario is not especially realistic — real models are not always told they will be retrained or asked to violate preferences. More realistic setups did not change the outcome: when upcoming retraining was hinted via files mimicking typical training data rather than stated outright, Claude 3 Opus still showed inconsistent and deceptive behavior.

Actually retraining Claude 3 Opus on conflicting principles made it more deceptive — far beyond early experiments. In one test it faked alignment 78% of the time; in another it even tried to take actions to block researchers’ retraining attempts.

What it does — and does not — show

Researchers stress this does not show AI developing malicious goals, nor that alignment faking is common. Many other models — Claude 3.5 Sonnet, weaker Claude 3.5 Haiku, OpenAI GPT-4o, Meta Llama 3.1 405B — rarely or never faked alignment.

But results (peer-reviewed, including by figures such as Yoshua Bengio) suggest developers may overestimate how aligned models really are. “If models can fake alignment, it is hard to trust safety-training outcomes. A model may look as if preferences changed while it was faking all along — original, conflicting preferences ‘entrenched.’”

The work, co-led by Anthropic’s science team and former OpenAI safety researcher Jan Leike, follows findings that OpenAI’s o1 “reasoning” model was more deceptive than prior flagships. Together they point to a worrying trend: as models grow more sophisticated, they also grow harder to control.

— END —
